title: What day is it today?
goal: Say days, dates, and years — and use the one pattern that runs through all of Mandarin: from big to small.
bekal: give days and dates in the correct Mandarin order
wish someone a happy birthday and handle invitations
tell 號 from 日, and read years digit by digit

dialogs.title: 對話 — 生日快樂
dialogs.intro: In the cafeteria, A-Ming asks Budi about a birthday, because they want to celebrate.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.id: Budi, what day is it today?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [真的|Zhēn de][嗎|ma]？[幾月|Jǐ yuè][幾號|jǐ hào]？

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: [五月|Wǔ yuè][十二號|shí'èr hào]，[星期三|xīngqísān]。

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: So what are we going to do?

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: [晚上|Wǎnshang][吃飯|chīfàn]，[然後|ránhòu][唱歌|chànggē]。[你|Nǐ][有空|yǒukòng][嗎|ma]？

lines.literal: evening — eat-rice, then — sing-song. you — have — time — (question)?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Yes! I want to give her a present.
lines.literal: have! I — want — give — her — one — (measure word) — gift.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.literal: good — main-idea! she — very — like — look-book.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [那|Nà][我|wǒ][送|sòng][她|tā][一本|yì běn][書|shū][好了|hǎo le]。
lines.id: Then I'll just give her a book.
lines.literal: then — I — give — her — one — (measure word) — book — good — (now).

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: ⚠️[不要|Bú yào][送|sòng][鐘|zhōng][喔|o]！[那|Nà][不吉利|bù jílì]。
lines.id: Just don't give her a clock! That's bad luck.
lines.literal: not — want — give — clock — (you know)! that — not — lucky.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: [送鐘|Sòng zhōng][聽起來|tīngqǐlái][像|xiàng][送終|sòngzhōng]，[很|hěn][不好|bù hǎo]。
lines.id: "Giving a clock" sounds like "seeing someone off to their death" — really bad.
lines.literal: give — clock — hear-up — like — see-off — end, very — not — good.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Wow, good thing you told me! I nearly put my foot in it.
lines.literal: wow, still — good — you — say! I — short-a-little — hit-disaster.

notes: ⚠️ **Never give a clock as a present to a Chinese speaker.** 送鐘 (*sòng zhōng*, give a clock) sounds exactly like 送終 (*sòngzhōng*, attend someone on their deathbed). This taboo is serious and holds across the whole Chinese-speaking world.

**Other gifts to avoid:** umbrellas (傘 *sǎn* sounds like 散 *sàn*, to split up), shoes (鞋 *xié* sounds like 邪 *xié*, evil), and knives or scissors (cutting ties). Safe gifts: food, fruit, tea, books, cosmetics.
**怎麼了？ means "what's wrong?", "what's up?"** — used when you notice something unusual. Don't confuse it with 為什麼 ("why", looking for a reason) and 怎麼樣 ("how is it").
**好了 at the end of a sentence means "…I'll just do that, then"** — a relaxed decision. *我送她一本書好了。* It's very common and makes you sound natural.
⚠️ **還好 has two meanings:** "luckily" (*還好你說*) and "OK, so-so" (the answer to 你好嗎?). Context separates them, and the second is the most honest and most common reply in Taiwan.

grammars.title: Days of the week: just count
body: Mandarin numbers its weekdays instead of naming them. **星期 ("week") + number** — and the count starts on Monday, not Sunday.
after: ⚠️ **Sunday is not 星期七.** That form doesn't exist. Use 星期日 (a bit formal, on calendars) or 星期天 (everyday).
⚠️ **期 in 星期 is read *qí* in Taiwan**, not *qī* as on the mainland. This tone difference is one of the most frequent markers of Taiwanese pronunciation, because the word is used every day.
**週 (*zhōu*) is a shorter, slightly formal form**: 週一, 週二, 週末 (weekend). You'll see it on timetables and notice boards.

grammars.title: Dates: month first, and always big to small
body: Mandarin gives dates in the order **year → month → date → weekday** — the reverse of English, which puts the weekday first and the year last ("Wednesday, May 12, 2026").

Pattern
Example
Pīnyīn
rows: 二〇二六年五月十二號星期三

after: ⚠️ **Years are read digit by digit, not as a number.** 2026 is *èr líng èr liù*, not *liǎngqiān líng èrshíliù*. This mistake is heard at once.
⚠️ **號 is for speaking, 日 for writing.** Calendars and formal letters use 日; everyday conversation always uses 號.
**Month names are just numbers**: 一月 January, 二月 February, through 十二月 December. No special names at all — a small gift that saves you twelve words.

⚠️ In Taiwan, official documents sometimes use **民國 (*Mínguó*)**, the Republic era: 2026 is 民國115年. The formula: Western year minus 1911. You'll see it on ID cards, train tickets, and official receipts.

sections.title: Time words that come in sets

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice that the pattern is **not uniform**: days use 昨/今/明, weeks and months use 上/這/下, and years use 去/今/明. The three sets must be learned separately, and mixing them (*上天* for yesterday) is a common mistake. **月 always needs 個** in between: 上**個**月, not 上月.

blocks.title: The song you'll hear
items: "Happy Birthday" is sung in Taiwan with Mandarin lyrics: **祝你生日快樂** (*Zhù nǐ shēngrì kuàilè*), repeated four times to exactly the same tune as the English version.
**Birthday cake** is 蛋糕 (*dàngāo*), and blowing out the candles is 吹蠟燭 (*chuī làzhú*).
⚠️ **Traditional birthdays follow the lunar calendar (農曆)**, so older Taiwanese often have two different birthday dates each year. Young people generally use the Western date.
**壽星** (*shòuxīng*, "star of long life") is what you call the person whose birthday it is. *今天你是壽星！*

blocks.text: Numbers in Taiwan aren't just numbers — their sound decides whether they're loved or avoided. This is no minor superstition: apartment prices, license plates, and hospital room numbers are genuinely affected.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Many buildings in Taiwan have no 4th floor**, jumping from 3 to 5 — just as Western buildings skip floor 13. Hospitals almost never have a room numbered 4. If you give a gift made up of several items, avoid four; **give two, six, or eight**.
